headline: State desk: Tennessee bill returns; Maine drops lounge push
dek: Tennessee Democrats will refile a legalization bill in 2027, Maine's lounge bill is shelved and Alaska weighs doubling concentrate limits on 18 November.
key_points: Tennessee Sen. Heidi Campbell says the Pot for Potholes Act, rejected 7-2 in committee in March, will return unchanged in 2027.
Maine Rep. David Boyer will not refile his cannabis lounge bill, which the House voted down 108-35 in April.
Alaska's Marijuana Control Board meets on 18 and 19 November on two plans that would raise the daily concentrate limit from 7 grams.
North Carolina's cannabis council met on 17 November; its draft report is due by 1 December and a final vote on 15 December.
body: The 2027 legislative sessions are already taking shape in the states, and the early signals are mixed. In Tennessee, Democrats say they will bring back a full legalization bill that failed in committee this year. In Maine, a Republican who championed cannabis lounges says he is giving up on his version. In Alaska and North Carolina, regulators and advisers are working through rules that will decide how much people can buy and who gets to sell it.
None of these moves changes the law today. Together they show where the next fights will be: social consumption, purchase limits, and how tightly a new market controls the number of stores.

State Sen. Heidi Campbell, a Democrat, told The Marijuana Herald on 17 November that she and Rep. Aftyn Behn, also a Democrat, will reintroduce the Pot for Potholes Act in the 2027 session. Supporters planned to meet on the evening of 18 November to prepare the new version, and Campbell said they have no plans to change it.

The 2026 bill, SB 2440 and HB 2525, would have let adults 21 and over possess up to 60 grams and grow up to 12 plants, with licensing run by the state Department of Agriculture. Purchases would carry a 15% tax on top of sales tax, with most of the money going to the state highway fund, which is where the bill's name comes from. The Senate Judiciary Committee rejected it 7-2 on 24 March, and the House version was taken off its subcommittee calendar a day later, according to the Herald.

Tennessee has no comprehensive medical cannabis programme, and its legislature is controlled by Republicans, so an unchanged bill faces the same arithmetic in 2027. The value for the industry is in the record: each failed vote shows which members are movable, and the 12-plant home-grow limit is generous next to many legal states.
## Maine: the lounge bill is shelved

Rep. David Boyer, a Republican, told the Herald he will not reintroduce his bill to allow cannabis hospitality lounges in 2027. The bill, LD 1365, would have let towns approve on-site consumption businesses. The House rejected it in April by voting 108-35 to accept the committee's recommendation that it ought not to pass. Boyer blamed opposition from Democratic lawmakers and Gov. Janet Mills.

Boyer said he would support a Democratic bill that allows smoking on site, but not an edibles-only model. Democrat Hannah Pingree won the governor's race this month and takes over from Mills in January, and Democrats widened their majorities, according to the Herald. Social clubs were part of the 2016 voter initiative that legalized adult-use cannabis in Maine before the legislature removed them, so the idea has a history there.
> Lounges keep losing in statehouses because they are the one part of legalization most voters can see from the street.
## Alaska: concentrate limits on the table

Alaska's Marijuana Control Board meets in Anchorage on 18 and 19 November to consider a 9 November staff memo with two ways to raise purchase limits, as we reported on 16 November. Today a customer can buy 1 ounce of flower, 7 grams of concentrate and 5,600 mg of THC in total per day.

The first version doubles the concentrate limit to 14 grams and the combined THC cap to 11,200 mg, with a 100-unit tracking system. The second sets equivalents: 1 ounce of flower equals 14 grams of concentrate equals 140 servings of 10 mg THC products. Both would replace the separate, lower limits for on-site consumption with standard retail limits. The board can approve either version, amend it, send it back to staff or close the project; approved rules then go to the Department of Law and out for public comment.
## North Carolina: council moves toward a report

North Carolina's Advisory Council on Cannabis met in Raleigh on 17 November. We could not find a public account of decisions taken at that meeting by the time of publication. Under its published schedule, a draft report is due by 1 December, a vote on 15 December and final recommendations to Gov. Josh Stein by 31 December. As we reported on 15 November, one model before the council would license about 400 private dispensaries supplied through a state warehousing system. An October SurveyUSA poll for WRAL and WSOC found 63% support for adult-use legalization and 74% for medical cannabis, according to the Herald.

Watch the Alaska board's vote this week and whether the rules go to public comment before the end of the year. Watch Tennessee's refiled bill number when pre-filing opens, and whether Maine Democrats bring their own on-site consumption bill under Gov. Pingree. In North Carolina, watch the 1 December draft for its retail model and store count.
